reference.source: GeneReviews / Bradley's Neurology in Clinical Practice
clinicalPearls: SPG4, caused by heterozygous SPAST variants encoding spastin, is the commonest cause of autosomal dominant hereditary spastic paraplegia and typically presents as a pure phenotype
The core picture is an insidiously progressive spastic paraparesis with lower-limb hyperreflexia, extensor plantar responses, and spasticity that usually exceeds weakness
Bladder urgency and mild dorsal-column sensory changes in the feet are common, whereas the upper limbs are relatively spared
Age at onset is highly variable even within a family, ranging from early childhood to late adulthood, with earlier-onset cases sometimes progressing more slowly
A minority develop complicating features such as cognitive decline or thin corpus callosum, blurring the pure/complicated boundary
Management is symptomatic, centring on antispasticity therapy, physiotherapy, and bladder care; disease-modifying treatment is not available
Genetic confirmation and counselling are important because of dominant inheritance with incomplete penetrance and marked intrafamilial variability
reference.pathophysiology: Hereditary spastic paraplegias are a group of disorders defined by length-dependent, retrograde degeneration of the longest corticospinal tract axons, producing the characteristic lower-limb-predominant spasticity. In SPG4 the SPAST gene encodes spastin, a microtubule-severing ATPase important for axonal transport, microtubule dynamics, and endoplasmic reticulum shaping. Loss-of-function or dominant-negative variants impair these functions, and the demanding metabolic and transport requirements of very long motor axons make their distal segments preferentially vulnerable, so the fibres supplying the legs degenerate first.
additionalDifferentials: Other genetic forms of hereditary spastic paraplegia (e.g. SPG3A, SPG7, SPG11)
Primary lateral sclerosis and other motor neurone disorders
Cervical or thoracic myelopathy from compression or structural lesion
Multiple sclerosis and other demyelinating myelopathy
Dopa-responsive dystonia mimicking spastic gait in children
Vitamin B12 deficiency or copper-deficiency myelopathy
additionalInvestigations: MRI of the brain and whole spine to exclude structural, demyelinating, or compressive causes
Targeted or panel-based genetic testing for SPAST and other HSP genes, including dosage analysis for exonic deletions/duplications
Serum vitamin B12, copper, and very-long-chain fatty acids to exclude treatable or metabolic mimics
Nerve conduction studies and EMG to assess for a peripheral component or alternative diagnoses
Urodynamic assessment where bladder symptoms are prominent
redFlags: Rapid progression or prominent weakness out of keeping with a pure spastic paraparesis, suggesting an alternative diagnosis
New sensory level, back pain, or sphincter loss indicating a compressive or inflammatory myelopathy
Marked bulbar, cognitive, or upper-limb involvement pointing to a complicated or non-HSP disorder
Asymmetry or fasciculations raising concern for motor neurone disease
reference.prognosis: SPG4 is slowly progressive over decades; many people remain ambulant with aids, and life expectancy is generally normal, although mobility and bladder function decline gradually and disability accrues with longer disease duration.
pitfalls: Attributing a treatable compressive or nutritional myelopathy to HSP without imaging and bloods
Assuming a negative family history excludes SPG4 given incomplete penetrance and de novo variants
Overlooking bladder dysfunction and its impact on quality of life
Expecting a uniform onset age within a family when intrafamilial variability is wide
management: Symptomatic antispasticity therapy with oral baclofen or tizanidine, escalating to intrathecal baclofen for severe refractory lower-limb spasticity
Botulinum toxin injection for focal spasticity restricting gait
Regular physiotherapy, stretching and provision of orthoses and walking aids to preserve ambulation and prevent contractures
Bladder care for urgency with antimuscarinic therapy and urodynamic assessment
Surveillance for progressive gait decline, contractures and, in a minority, cognitive change or thin corpus callosum
Genetic counselling for autosomal dominant inheritance with highly variable age at onset, offering predictive testing to relatives
Multidisciplinary neurology, physiotherapy, occupational therapy and continence services
